newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT-Australian 10-yr bond finds base in SYCOM.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Australian 10-yr bond finds base in SYCOM.

text.p: *The Australian 10-year bond futures contract stabilised in SYCOM after the recent correction from extreme overbought levels, ending with modest gains.
*Contract seen in a 93.270/93.360 range on the day.
*U.S. Treasuries little changed, retail sales up 0.5 pct.

The September Australian 10-year bond futures contract found a tentative base in after-hours trade after the recent correction from extreme overbought levels, ending with modest gains over Tuesday's pit close.
The contract finished SYCOM at 93.300, up from an open outcry close of 93.270, and having touched a low of 93.235 at one stage.

The 14-day relative strength index on the 10-year bond has now wound back to around 70 percent having breached 80 percent last week which coincided with the contract touching a 3-1/2 year high of 93.415.
Peter Pontikis, technical strategist at Westpac, expects the contract to be limited in a 93.270/93.360 range or narrower.

"(The 10-year bond) has relieved itself of its overbought condition. For the day, technicals suggest a mild improvement, but to stay away from first resistance in the likely beginning of a consolidation pattern sideways...," Pontikis said.

The local market was underpinned by a stable finish in U.S. Treasuries with June U.S. retail sales failing to make much impression. The data showed a 0.5 percent rise, a tad above expectations, but was accompanied by a downward revision to minus 0.3 percent from down 0.1 percent in the May report.
The U.S. market faces a barrage of data later on Wednesday with June CPI, along with May business inventories, industrial production and capacity utilisation all due for release.

Locally, data remains thin, although Westpac's latest consumer sentiment survey at 2.30 p.m. (0430 GMT) may generate more interest than usual given that it has fallen three consecutive months to its lowest level since September 1995.
"If it (the index) slips below 100.0 that will be quite soft territory...and it may give more direction than it usually does," said Stephen Roberts chief economist at UBS Australia.
